solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Straight entertainers with stuffing knocked out by a funny show (2,2,5)

indicators.note: the word's filling is removed, leaving only its two ends

blocks.note: the article, taken as it is
ENTERTAINERS without everything between E and S

annotation.surface: A comedy act gets beaten up by a sitcom's stars, or the stuffing is knocked out of some straight-man entertainers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Straight' is the barman's word: a spirit served straight is served as it comes, with nothing added. 'Entertainers' looks like the show's cast, but only its two end letters are used.
annotation.definitionFit: A drink taken straight is served as it comes, neat and unmixed.

clue.text: Answer that’s not filled in, understood in secret language (5)

indicators.note: the word is left empty, keeping only its first and last letters

blocks.note: ANSWER with its middle NSWE left blank

annotation.surface: A crossword answer left blank because it was only understood in some secret code.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface nods at an unfilled grid square, which is exactly what happens to ANSWER: its inside is left empty.
annotation.definitionFit: Argot is the private jargon of a group, a language outsiders cannot follow.

clue.text: Dip very short tongue? (7)

blocks.note: 1 mm, one millimetre, is a very short length; the 1 becomes I

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether a dip is a very short tongue, as if it were a quick lick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very short' is a measurement, not an adjective: one millimetre, written 1MM, with the digit read as I. 'Tongue' means a language, not the thing in your mouth.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean plunging something under the surface of a liquid.

clue.text: Suit hosting party concerned with vegetarian food (9)

indicators.note: the suit takes the other letters in as guests

blocks.note: a suit is a legal case

annotation.surface: A businessman in a suit throws a party for a vegetarian cause.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suit' looks like clothing but is a lawsuit, CASE, which holds LAB + RE. Calabrese is the green sprouting broccoli.
annotation.definitionFit: Calabrese is a type of broccoli, so vegetable food fit for vegetarians.

clue.text: Newsworthy story best friend chewed over here? (3,5,3)

definitions.text: Newsworthy story best friend chewed over here?

blocks.note: the surface wants any headline; the setter means the journalists' textbook example of a story worth printing
the surface suggests a pal being discussed; the setter means man's best friend literally being bitten, by his owner

annotation.surface: A newspaper editor weighs a story about somebody's best friend being chewed.
annotation.walkthrough: The journalists' saying: 'dog bites man' is no news, but 'man bites dog' is. The dog is man's best friend, here chewed by its owner.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase is a newsroom byword for an unusual event that makes a good story.

clue.text: Sponge cakes go flat in the end (3)

indicators.note: take the end of each word

blocks.note: last letters of cakeS gO flaT

annotation.surface: A sponge cake sinks in the oven and ends up flat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sponge' seems to be a cake, but it is a drunkard: someone who soaks up drink.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang by image: a sponge soaks up liquid, so it means a habitual drunkard, which the old word here names.

clue.text: Split blades (5)

blocks.note: British slang: to split on someone is to inform on them to the police
the narrow green leaves of a lawn grow as blades

annotation.surface: A knife blade split in two.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Split' and 'grass' are both British slang for informing to the police; a grass is an informer.
annotation.definitionFit: To split or grass is to tell on someone; grass also grows in blades.

clue.text: I’m disgusted by 24 six-packs? (5)

definitions.note: 'I'm disgusted' is a whole sentence; GROSS stands in as the exclamation 'Gross!'

blocks.note: the one-word exclamation that says this

annotation.surface: Someone is appalled at a pile of 24 six-packs, whether of beer or of abdominal muscles.
annotation.walkthrough: The arithmetic is the trick: 24 packs of six make 144, which is a gross, twelve dozen.
annotation.definitionFit: A gross is twelve dozen, 144, and 'Gross!' voices disgust.

clue.text: Infidel witnessing robbery? (7)

annotation.surface: An unbeliever happens to see a robbery take place.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition-free reading, 'at heist', is a pun on the word itself.
annotation.definitionFit: An infidel is someone without religious faith, as an atheist is.

clue.text: Part of scrum down, score after collapse (6,3)

indicators.note: the letters fall into a new order once the scrum collapses

annotation.surface: A rugby scrum goes down and the team scores after it collapses.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word here is rugby, so the anagram fodder hides in plain sight. The second row are the forwards in the middle of a rugby scrum.
annotation.definitionFit: The second row is one of the three rows of forwards that make up a rugby scrum.

clue.text: Percussion ensemble with something to play, short track (7)

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: a game is something you play
LANE, a track, without its E

annotation.surface: A drum band arrives with something to play: a short track.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Play' and 'track' pull toward music, but GAME is a game and LANE is a path. A gamelan is the Indonesian orchestra of gongs and metallophones.
annotation.definitionFit: A gamelan is a traditional Indonesian ensemble made up mostly of percussion instruments.

clue.text: Parallel eating habits originally related to nutrition (7)

indicators.note: the outer word swallows the letter
take the original, first letter

blocks.note: the tropics are parallels of latitude

annotation.surface: A study finds matching eating habits that trace back to diet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eating habits' reads as a single diet phrase, but 'eating' is the container instruction: TROPIC eats H.
annotation.definitionFit: Trophic describes feeding and nutrition, as in trophic levels of a food chain.

clue.text: Beat time, having raised orchestral baton first of all (5)

indicators.note: the first letter of all the words before it

blocks.clueFragment: having raised orchestral baton first of all
blocks.note: first letters of Having Raised Orchestral Baton

annotation.surface: A conductor lifts the baton before beating time for the orchestra.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beat time' reads as the conductor's job, but 'Beat' is the definition and 'time' only supplies T.
annotation.definitionFit: A throb is a strong regular beat, like a pulse.

clue.text: I go in nest, after flying about, for feeding (9)

indicators.note: the letters are scattered around and land in a new order

annotation.surface: A bird explains it returns to the nest after flying around, to feed its chicks.
annotation.walkthrough: The bird picture makes 'flying about' look like part of the story rather than an instruction to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Ingestion is the taking in of food, the act of feeding.

clue.text: Beastly thing and gruesome display for the audience (7,4)

indicators.note: the words are to be heard, not read

annotation.surface: A horror show puts something beastly and gruesome on stage for the audience.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' seems to mean nasty but is literal: a beast, the animal.
annotation.definitionFit: A grizzly bear is literally a beast, a large North American brown bear.

clue.text: Sweet or savoury dish, mixed type (3)

blocks.note: a baked pastry dish with a fruit or meat filling
printers' term for metal type spilled into a jumble

annotation.surface: A menu entry for a dish that could go either way, sweet or savoury.
annotation.walkthrough: The second sense is old printing jargon: 'pie' (or 'pi') is metal type spilled into a jumble.
annotation.definitionFit: A pie can be sweet or savoury, and pie is also jumbled printer's type.

clue.text: Lit up — as ceilings, perhaps? (9)

blocks.note: ceilings are usually coated with a smooth lime or gypsum finish

annotation.surface: A room with its ceilings lit up by lamps.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lit up' pairs naturally with ceilings as lighting, but it is slang for drunk.
annotation.definitionFit: Lit up and plastered are both slang for very drunk.

clue.text: Heavenly body gave interns breaks (7,4)

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and reassembled

annotation.surface: A gorgeous boss let the interns take breaks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly body' reads as someone attractive, which makes the office scene plausible, but it is a planet. The evening star is usually Venus.
annotation.definitionFit: The evening star, usually Venus, is a heavenly body shining after sunset.

clue.text: Drink large rum and energy drink (6,3)

indicators.note: rum as an adjective means odd, so the letters come out strangely arranged

annotation.surface: An order at the bar: a drink, a large rum and an energy drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the spirit but works as the adjective meaning odd, so LARGE is to be jumbled. The first 'Drink' is wordplay; the last one is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Ginger ale is a fizzy ginger-flavoured soft drink.

clue.text: One drink, Australian opening port, nothing special (1,4,1,5)

indicators.note: the other letters open up the port and go inside it

annotation.surface: An Australian opens a port bar and serves a drink that turns out to be nothing special.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opening' looks like a first-letter instruction, but the three pieces prise the port apart and sit inside it. The port is in Yemen.
annotation.definitionFit: An American idiom: goods selling at ten cents for twelve are so plentiful they are ordinary.

clue.text: Picture this writer and soldier in shock (7)

indicators.note: the soldier sits inside the shock

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as I
a shock of hair, a mane
a GI is an American soldier

annotation.surface: A writer pictures themself alongside a soldier suffering from shell shock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shock' reads as trauma, but a shock of hair is a thick mass of it, and the soldier sits inside that.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean forming a mental image of something.

clue.text: Only a handful I’m relieved to hear? (3)

indicators.note: 'to hear' tells the solver to listen to the words rather than read them, so they count by their sound

blocks.note: 'Phew!' is what you say when relieved

annotation.surface: Someone is relieved to hear there are only a handful of something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'm relieved' stands for the exclamation itself, 'Phew!', not a description of a feeling.
annotation.definitionFit: Few means only a small number, a handful.

clue.text: Complex pattern generated by craft adrift on American lake (7)

indicators.note: the letters of craft float out of place
in a down clue, one piece is placed after another

annotation.surface: A boat drifting on an American lake leaves an intricate wake pattern.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Craft' is a boat, which makes 'adrift' read as description rather than an instruction to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A fractal is an endlessly complex, self-similar pattern.

clue.text: Drink separately in fun (9)

annotation.surface: A suggestion to drink on your own, just for fun.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is an adverb phrase, so the answer must be one too: done teasingly is done in fun.
annotation.definitionFit: To say something teasingly is to say it in fun.

clue.text: Introduce class who are popular? (5)

blocks.note: a set is a class or group
surface padding that makes the class a group of people

annotation.surface: A teacher introduces the class of cool kids.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'in set' are the popular crowd, which is why the clue reads as a school scene; the question mark covers the reversed word order.
annotation.definitionFit: To inset something is to put it in, to introduce it into something else.

clue.text: Camel leaving river with antelope (5)

indicators.note: the river departs from the word, taking its letters with it

blocks.note: CAMEL without CAM, the river through Cambridge

annotation.surface: A camel wanders off from the river alongside an antelope.
annotation.walkthrough: The Cam is the Cambridge river, a crossword favourite. An eland is a large African antelope.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the answer is one species, the largest spiral-horned kind on the African savanna.

clue.text: Hat raised, lifted with courtesy, ultimately (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, the word goes up, so it reads backwards
'ultimately' means in the end, so only the word's final letter counts

blocks.note: raised = BRED, which then goes up the grid

annotation.surface: A gentleman raises and lifts his hat as a courtesy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Raised' and 'lifted' look like the same hat-tipping gesture twice, but one means bred (children are raised) and the other reverses it.
annotation.definitionFit: A derby is a bowler hat, especially in American usage.

clue.text: Queen rejected by girl, possibly put out again? (7)

indicators.note: turned back, so ER reads RE
a girl is one example of issue

blocks.note: a daughter is one's issue, one's offspring

annotation.surface: A queen is spurned by a girl who may be thrown out again.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Issue' in the sense of offspring is legal and royal language; a girl is one possible kind.
annotation.definitionFit: To reissue something is to put it out again, like a record or a book.

clue.text: Old letter delivered in time, thankfully (3)

indicators.note: the letter arrives tucked inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: An old letter arrives on time, to everyone's relief.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Letter' is not post but an alphabet character: eth (ð) is an Old English letter, still used in Icelandic.
annotation.definitionFit: Eth is an obsolete letter of the Old English alphabet.

clue.text: Demanding individual, one no longer taking a part? (7)

blocks.note: a performer takes a part in a play
surface padding naming the person described

annotation.surface: A fussy person who used to play roles is being described.
annotation.walkthrough: Read EXACTOR as 'ex-actor', someone who no longer takes parts; 'no longer' sits inside the actor phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: An exactor is someone who exacts, demanding what is due.

clue.text: Raised mark on back of hand resided (5)

indicators.note: the last letter of the word
in an across clue, WELT is put against D

blocks.note: a welt is a raised mark on the skin

annotation.surface: A raised welt appeared on the back of someone's hand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back of hand' reads as anatomy, where a welt might sit, but it just means the final letter of HAND.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: both mean having lived in a place.

clue.text: High jinks in Equus, perhaps (9)

blocks.note: Equus is Peter Shaffer's play about horses

annotation.surface: Some rowdy behaviour breaks out during a performance of Equus.
annotation.walkthrough: Equus (Latin for horse) is a Peter Shaffer stage play about a boy who blinds horses, so it is literally a horse play.
annotation.definitionFit: Horseplay is rough, boisterous fun, just like high jinks.
